persons.note: PROJECTED RESIDENT. Documented in Chicago post-office evidence but not independently corroborated strongly enough for attested circa-1835 residence. The papers print 'Chesnut, Jules' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 20 May 1835, column 13 — dated 1835-05-20. Nothing else in the corpus names this person: no trade, no street, no household, no arrival, so every other claim here is written unattested in its own block. persons.name: H. B. Clarke
persons.note: A DOCUMENTED PERSON, AND NOTHING ELSE IS CLAIMED. The papers name 'H, B, CLARKE' and 'H. B. CLARKE' and 'H. Bh CLARKE' and 'Wo, CLARKE' and give the trade; they do not say where this household lived, who else was in it, or when it came. So the record around this person carries nothing but the person: no dwelling, no division, no family, each written as unattested in its own block rather than filled in from the shape of the rest of the town. Cited at the Democrat of 27 May 1835, column 5; the Democrat of 8 July 1835, column 9; the Democrat of 22 July 1835, column 9; the Democrat of 29 July 1835, column 12. The corpus associates the name with Chicago, South Water Street; that is where the paper does business with this person and not a statement about where they slept, and the storefront tickets are the ones that may stand a shop there. THE TOWN NEVER INVENTED A ROOF FOR THIS TRADE. The occupation census raised reconstructed households for the trades a town of 3,265 people needed and could not document; `hardware_merchant` was not one of them, which is why this person could only ever be ADDED and never seated on an existing record — data/research/newspapers/register_1835.json calls it `new_resident` for exactly that reason. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1). READ THROUGH A TRANSCRIPTION, not a scan: the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 grades a transcription-mediated reading as documented, and the source record for the run states that standard and its limits. A scan read that confirms or corrects the name upgrades this entry. FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the poll of Chicago's first city election, 2 May 1837 — “Henry B. Clarke,” (f1839_v0010, printed page 41, ward 1, voting for William B. Ogden). What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago on 2 May 1837 and in that ward. It is written as 1837 evidence with describes_date 1837-05-02, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected_resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. The ward is a location in the CITY of 1837, whose six wards are drawn on printed page 46; it is not a location in the town of 1835 and does not place a house. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Clarke' folds to the same string as the 1837 entry's, and the given name of both begins H. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_election_crosswalk_1835.json and fergus_1839_register_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

residents.research_note: MINTED FROM THE NEWSPAPER REGISTER (T-0376), AND THE HOUSEHOLD IS A CONTAINER RATHER THAN AN ARGUMENT. Every other record in this dataset argues for a household — a family the sources count, or a trade the town demonstrably needed. This one argues for a PERSON: the Democrat and the American name H. B. Clarke as a hardware merchant at Chicago 4 time(s), and this reconstruction did not hold them. `data/residents/` has no way to carry a person except inside a household, so one was written around them and told to claim nothing: one member, no dwelling, no division, no origin, no arrival beyond the bound the paper sets. Reading a family, a house or a quarter of town into this record would be reading something the papers do not say. tools/mint_documented_residents.py derives the whole minted set and prints every candidate it refused, with the reason.

persons.name: Stephen Mack
persons.note: GRADED BY THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER — rule G1c, applied 2026-09-04. This identity is attested because that rung fired on the civic and press rows recorded on this card, which the resident-research corpus does not read. This programme's letter-list rule of 2026-09-02 would call it a projected resident on the absence of a research row; it is superseded here, and a no-find in one corpus is not a finding about another (T-0822). KNOWN ONLY FROM THE POST OFFICE, AND HELD THERE MORE THAN ONCE. The papers print 'Mack, Stephen' and 'Stephen Mack' in 2 separate returns of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 1 April 1834, column 2; the Democrat of 20 May 1835, column 13 — across 1834-04-01 to 1835-05-20. A name in a LATER return is somebody still being written to, months on, which is the strongest thing a letter list can say about residence and is why this person outranks a single-return name of the same surname. Nothing else in the corpus names this person: no trade, no street, no household, no arrival, so every other claim here is written unattested in its own block. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (docs/LIBERTIES.md L214), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py). No figure is drawn (L1). THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Mack, Stephen” (tax_1833_070, line 122). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Mack' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json).

citations.citation: The Chicago Democrat. Vol. I, No. 1 (November 26, 1833) through Vol. II, No. 18 (August 26, 1835). Chicago, Ill.: John Calhoun, editor and publisher. Seventy-three issues, OCR-assisted research transcriptions from page scans.
what_it_supplies: that a named trade was being carried on in Chicago in a named week, and often where
self-reported addresses, which are the strongest address evidence this project has: the advertiser was paying, and his customers had to find him
dissolution, removal and replacement notices — the only thing that keeps a documented business out of the 1835 town under the owner's ruling 3
post-office letter lists, naming residents by the hundred (ruling 1: a listed name mints a resident candidate, flagged letter_list_only)
the village and later town ordinances, printed complete — the 7 November 1833 code is the richest single item in the run
arrivals and clearances, which date the piers and the harbour as working structures
public notices that fix a building as a polling place, an auction site or a meeting place on a given day
the paper's own imprint, self-reported: the corner of South Water and Clark streets
twenty-one months of continuous weekly attestation ending three weeks before the scene date, including the issue printed on 1835-07-01
what_it_does_not_supply: any building's form, material, storey count, fenestration or dimensions — an advertisement describes a trade, not a building
the specific corner of any junction it names: 'on the corner of' does not say which of the four
anything at all from an engraving — see trap 1; the cuts are the printer's stock
proof that a business named in 1833 or 1834 still stood on 1835-07-01; that is ruling 3's survival liberty, and it is a liberty
an argument from silence, unless corpus.json shows the issues either side of the silence are both in the deposit
a reading that outranks a scan read of the same passage — see ruling 2 and the C. & I. HARMON case
a citation without an issue page and column

citations.citation: Chicago · July 1835: Building Inventory and Architectural Reconstruction Specification. Prepared for Kevin Haas, August 2026.
what_it_supplies: A 665-roof production target with independently reconcilable group, district, level, and construction totals.
Thirty-five architectural family definitions with dimensional and massing bands.
District character, spacing, variation, finish, and chronology constraints for a July 1835 reconstruction.
A required distinction between named documentary landmarks and anonymous inferred infill.
what_it_does_not_supply: A surviving July 1835 building census or parcel-by-parcel roof register.
Exact locations, dimensions, appearance, occupants, or construction dates for anonymous roofs.
Authority to replace stronger building-specific evidence already represented in the dataset.

research_note: RECONSTRUCTED / GENERATED, NOT AN ATTESTED NAMED BUILDING. Family and aggregate district role follow the owner-supplied 2026 specification; exact presence, location, footprint, finish and instance-level form are interpretive.

fabric_basis.words: whitewashed clapboard on a balloon frame, 12-over-12 sash of 6 × 8 in glass and plain corner boards, under a weathered roof — The Bradford household's, in Chicago since 1834 (rule F-T)
